blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** Caching. **Goal:** make reads fast without lying about data, and without a cache taking down your system.
Recall the latency ladder:
Caching moves the answer from "slow store + network" to "fast store, often local". A cache hit that avoids a 5 ms DB round trip is a 50x latency improvement on that operation.
**But caching is not free.** Every cache adds: invalidation complexity, a staleness contract, a new failure mode, memory cost, and a second source of truth.
**The rule:** add a cache when you have *measured* that the origin is too slow or too loaded, and you can state the staleness you're willing to accept.

blocks.code:
User Browser
  └─ (1) HTTP cache / Service Worker      [seconds–hours, per-user]
       └─ (2) CDN / Edge cache            [minutes–hours, global PoPs]
            └─ (3) Reverse proxy cache     [seconds–minutes, per-DC]
                 └─ (4) Application cache   [seconds–minutes, Redis/Memcached]
                      └─ (5) Local/in-process cache [milliseconds, per-node]
                           └─ Origin (DB / API)

blocks.text: Add layers from the top down. Each layer you add is one more place data can be stale.

rows: DB result caching, sessions, hot objects

sections.title: 3. The caching patterns (the four you must know)

blocks.text: Cache-aside (lazy loading) — **the default**

rows: Cache failure ≠ data loss (origin is authoritative)
Stale until TTL expires or explicit invalidation

blocks.text: Read-through
The cache itself fetches from the origin on a miss. The app only talks to the cache.

rows: Cache implementation is coupled to the origin

blocks.text: Write-through
Writes go to the cache, which writes through to the origin and updates the cache.

rows: Read path is always a hit

blocks.text: Write-around / write-behind (write-back)
**Write-around:** write to the origin; on a subsequent read, the cache is populated. **Write-behind:** write to the cache, update the origin asynchronously.

rows: Write-behind: fast writes, absorbs write bursts
**Write-behind can lose data** if the cache dies before the async write lands
Write-around: avoids caching data nobody reads
Cache and origin can drift badly

blocks.text: **Write-behind is only safe if the cache is durable** (persisted, replicated) and the window is bounded. Otherwise a cache restart loses committed writes. Most production systems avoid it for anything users care about.
Refresh-ahead
Refresh a hot entry in the background shortly *before* it expires, so users never wait for a miss.
When the cache is full, something must go.

rows: Zipfian workloads (a few hot items dominate)
Data with a known staleness bound
Approximate LRU with a reference bit
Best hit rate for real workloads (used by Caffeine, RocksDB)

blocks.text: Why LRU is hard

Strict LRU requires maintaining a global recency order — O(log N) with a balanced tree, or O(1) with a linked list, but either way it's a **write-heavy, cache-unfriendly** data structure. Real systems approximate it:

items.text: **Redis**: approximates LRU with *sampled LRU* — it samples a few random keys on each eviction

blocks.text: and evicts the coldest of the sample. O(1), nearly as good.

items.text: **Redis 4+**: adds LFU with a logarithmic counter.

blocks.text: The scan problem

A full table scan of 1M keys evicts the entire hot set under LRU. Fixes: **SLRU** (new items go to a probationary segment and must prove popularity before entering the protected segment) or **TinyLFU** (frequency sketch resists one-hit scans).
Memory management

items.text: **Set a memory limit** (`maxmemory` in Redis) and an eviction policy. Never let the cache OOM

blocks.text: the box.

items.text: **Account for overhead**: Redis entries have per-item overhead (~50–100 bytes plus allocator

blocks.text: slack). A 1 KB value may cost 1.3 KB.

items.text: **Don't cache huge objects.** Cache a pointer/ID, not a 10 MB blob.

blocks.text: There are exactly two ways to keep a cache correct:

items.text: **Expire it** (TTL) — bounded staleness, no coordination.
**Invalidate it explicitly** — exact, but requires knowing when data changes.

blocks.text: TTL (time-based expiry)

rows: May serve stale data for an unacceptable window
May expire data that's still hot (wasted work)

blocks.text: **Choosing a TTL:** it should be derived from the **staleness the business can tolerate**, not from a round number. If a price may be shown up to 30 seconds stale → TTL 30s. If a user's own profile must be current → don't cache it, or invalidate on write.
**Jitter TTLs** to avoid a thundering herd of simultaneous expirations.
Explicit invalidation

rows: Simple; breaks if the delete fails or races
Write publishes "key X changed"; subscribers delete
Needs a bus; messages can be lost
Don't invalidate at all; bound staleness with TTL

blocks.text: The classic race

blocks.code:
Request A: reads DB (old value 1)
Request B: writes DB (new value 2), then DEL cache key
Request A: SET cache key = 1     ← stale value re-inserted AFTER the delete

blocks.text: **Fixes:**

items.text: **Delete after the DB write commits** (not before) — reduces but doesn't eliminate the window.
**Write-through** — the write updates the cache directly, so there's no stale re-insert.
**Versioned keys / cache-aside with a version check**: on write, bump a version counter; the

blocks.text: reader writes to `key:v{N}` only if the version is still current (Lua script for atomicity).

items.text: **Locking** — a per-key mutex around read+fill.
**Short TTL** — bounds the damage.
**"Delete late"** — delay the delete slightly so in-flight stale writes land first, then delete.

blocks.text: **The most robust simple pattern:** write-through cache + TTL. The write path updates both store and cache atomically-ish, and the TTL is the safety net for any missed invalidation.
These four bugs account for most cache-related incidents.
Cache penetration (miss on a key that doesn't exist)
Attack or accident sends requests for keys that never exist. Every request misses the cache and hits the DB.
**Fixes:**

items.text: **Cache negative results** (store a sentinel for "not found", short TTL).
**Bloom filter** of valid keys: if the key isn't in the filter, don't touch the DB.
**Validate input format** before lookup (reject malformed IDs early).
**Rate limit** and **WAF** rules on the endpoint.

blocks.text: Cache avalanche (all keys expire at once)
At midnight, every key's TTL ends simultaneously → the DB takes 100% of the traffic.
**Fixes:**

items.text: **Jittered TTLs** (TTL = base ± random).
**Staggered warm-up** after a cold start.
**Refresh-ahead** for hot keys.
**Circuit breaker / bulkhead**: limit how many cache misses may hit the DB concurrently; serve

blocks.text: stale data instead.

items.text: **Serve stale while revalidating** (stale-while-revalidate).

blocks.text: Cache stampede / thundering herd (one hot key misses, many requests hit the DB)
One very popular key expires; 10,000 concurrent requests all miss and all query the DB, then all write to the cache.
**Fixes:**

items.text: **Request coalescing / single-flight**: only one thread populates the cache; the others wait

blocks.text: (singleflight, `go-cache/singleflight`, `cache.get_or_set` in Laravel, `Cache.get(key, fn)` with locking).

items.text: **Distributed lock** around the fill (with a timeout).
**Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)**: refresh slightly before expiry, with a random

blocks.text: early-return probability, so only one request refreshes.

items.text: **Stale-while-revalidate**: serve the stale value immediately, refresh in the background.

blocks.text: Cache breakdown (the cache is down, the DB dies too)
Every request falls through to the DB at 100x the normal rate → DB overload → total outage.
**Fixes:**

items.text: **Circuit breaker**: after N failures, stop trying the cache (or the DB) and fail fast.
**Bulkhead**: limit concurrent fallthrough requests to the origin.
**Fail-open vs fail-closed** — decide per dependency:
*Cache down*: usually **fail-open** (go to the DB, slower but correct) — unless the DB can't take the load, then serve stale/degraded.
*Auth service down*: often **fail-closed** (deny) for security, or use a cached token list.
**Degraded modes**: serve stale cache entries, reduce functionality.

blocks.text: **The cache must never be a hard dependency of the read path.** Its absence should reduce performance, not availability. Design for that from the start.

rows: You want the app to know only one store
Big scale; L1 must be invalidated on L2 change

blocks.text: Local (in-process) caches have a special problem

Each node has its own copy, so invalidation must be broadcast to all nodes (Redis pub/sub, Kafka topic). Messages can be lost or arrive late → **local cache TTLs should be short** and local caches should hold only data that's safe to be slightly stale.
Redis is the default distributed cache. Things that bite people:

rows: A slow command (big `KEYS`, huge `HGETALL`, `SORT`) blocks everything. Use `SCAN`, `UNLINK` (async delete), `lazyfree-lazy-user-del`
Set TTLs on everything; `maxmemory` + a policy
Store hashes instead of giant strings; cap value size
Redis persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF) is not a durability guarantee. Don't put unrecoverable data there
`maxmemory-policy noeviction` + bigger box, or `allkeys-lru` for a pure cache
One key receiving 100k ops/sec. Add replicas with `READONLY` and read from replicas, or shard the value
Never use `BLPOP` on the same connection pool serving normal traffic
Hash slots: multi-key ops need the same slot (use hash tags `{userId}`)
Redis Cluster uses async replication → acknowledged writes can be lost. Use `WAIT` or `min-replicas-to-write` if you need durability

blocks.text: Redis vs Memcached

items.text: **Memcached**: simpler, multi-threaded, pure cache, no persistence, no data structures.
**Redis**: more data structures, persistence, pub/sub, streams (a queue!), Lua scripting.

blocks.text: Use Memcached if you only need get/set and want simple multi-threaded throughput. Use Redis if you need any of the above.
Cache keys: design rules

items.text: Namespace by type: `user:{id}:v1`, `feed:home:{id}`
**Include a schema/version** in the key (`v1`) so you can invalidate everything by changing the

blocks.text: version — a **"cache busting"** trick that beats per-key invalidation for deploys.

items.text: Don't put secrets or PII in key names (keys are logged and visible).
Keep keys short — they're stored in memory repeatedly.

blocks.text: For anything static or semi-static, the CDN is the most effective cache you have.

items.text: **Cache key**: typically URL + selected headers. **Never** cache `Set-Cookie` responses for

blocks.text: shared caches, or you serve one user's data to another.

items.text: **Cache-Control directives**:
`max-age=3600` — fresh for an hour
`s-maxage=86400` — shared caches may reuse for a day (browser ignores)
`no-cache` — must revalidate (can still store)
`no-store` — don't store at all
`private` — only the browser may store it
`immutable` — won't change; use with content-hashed filenames
`stale-while-revalidate=600` — serve stale for 10 min while refreshing
`stale-if-error=86400` — serve stale if the origin is down
**Content hashing**: `app.4f3a2b1c.js` — new content = new URL = no purge needed. This is the

blocks.text: right way to deploy assets.

items.text: **Purge**: targeted invalidation via API (costs money, can be slow). Prefer hash-based URLs.

items.text: **Cache-aside with a TTL and metrics.** Wrap a DB call in a cache. Track hit ratio, p50/p99 latency of hits vs. misses, and the number of DB queries served. Then change the TTL and re-measure. Plot hit ratio vs. TTL.
**Reproduce cache stampede.** A hot key with a 1s TTL under 100 concurrent requesters. Count DB queries per second. Then implement single-flight (coalescing) and re-measure.
**Reproduce cache avalanche.** 10,000 keys all with the same TTL. Watch the DB get hammered at the expiry moment. Add jitter and re-measure.

**Race condition lab.** Two concurrent requests: one reads, one writes + invalidates. Loop 10,000 times and count how often the stale value survives in the cache. Then implement write-through and re-run.

**Local cache + pub/sub invalidation.** A Caffeine-style local cache in front of Redis, with invalidation broadcast over Redis pub/sub. Kill a subscriber mid-flight and observe stale local entries — then shorten the local TTL and observe the tradeoff.

blocks.text: Good: "Reads dominate, so I'll put a Redis cache in front of Postgres using cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL — the data changes every 5 minutes so that's the staleness we can accept. I'll invalidate on write as well to improve freshness. I'll monitor hit ratio and fall back to the DB with a circuit breaker if Redis is down."

Better: "For the hot item detail page I'll use refresh-ahead with stale-while-revalidate so users never wait on a fill, and I'll coalesce concurrent misses with singleflight so we don't stampede the DB. The static assets go to the CDN with hashed URLs, so deploys don't need purges."
Red flags: caching with no invalidation strategy; cache as a hard dependency; no consideration of the stampede; "we'll use Redis, it's fast" with no TTL/hit-ratio reasoning.

selfCheck.q: **Name the four cache pathologies and one fix for each.**
selfCheck.a: **Penetration** (requests for nonexistent keys always miss) → cache negative results, bloom filter, input validation. **Avalanche** (all keys expire together) → jittered TTLs, staggered warm-up, serve-stale. **Stampede/thundering herd** (many concurrent misses on one hot key) → single-flight/request coalescing, refresh-ahead, stale-while-revalidate. **Breakdown** (cache down → origin overloaded → total outage) → circuit breaker, bulkhead, fail-open with degraded serving.

selfCheck.q: **Cache-aside vs write-through: which one risks a stale value being written back after invalidation, and what's the standard fix?**
selfCheck.a: **Cache-aside.** The classic race: a reader fills the cache with a stale value right after a writer invalidated it. Standard fixes: write-through (the write updates the cache directly), delete-after-commit, versioned keys with an atomic check, per-key locking, or a short TTL as a backstop.

From the **business staleness tolerance**: "how wrong may this be, and for how long?" If the price may be 30 seconds stale, TTL = 30s. Also consider the cost of a miss (expensive fill → longer TTL) and the memory pressure. Never pick TTLs arbitrarily.

selfCheck.q: **Why does LRU need sampling in Redis?**
selfCheck.a: Strict LRU requires maintaining an exact global recency order, which is write-intensive and cache-hostile. Redis samples a few random keys per eviction and evicts the coldest of the sample — O(1) cost, near-LRU hit rate.

selfCheck.q: **What is the scan problem, and which policies resist it?**
selfCheck.a: A bulk scan (e.g. reading a whole table) inserts many one-hit entries that, under LRU, evict the genuinely hot set. SLRU (probationary/protected segments) and TinyLFU (frequency sketch) resist it.

selfCheck.q: **What is cache breakdown and why is it worse than a cache miss?**
selfCheck.a: With the cache down, 100% of requests fall through to the origin at 100x normal rate, so the origin is overloaded and the whole system fails — the cache's failure becomes the origin's outage. A cache *miss* is contained; a cache *outage* is not, unless you have a circuit breaker and bulkhead.

Write-behind updates the origin asynchronously. If the cache loses the data (restart, eviction, failover) before the async write lands, **committed data is lost**. It's only acceptable for data that's reproducible or tolerant of loss, and only with a durable cache.

selfCheck.q: **What is fail-open vs fail-closed, and which do you want when the cache is down?**
selfCheck.a: **Fail-open** = fall back to the origin (slower, but correct). **Fail-closed** = reject the request. For a cache, usually fail-open (with a bulkhead) — unless the origin can't absorb the load, in which case fail *degraded* (serve stale) or reject.

selfCheck.q: **A cache key is `user:123`. Why include a version like `user:123:v2`?**
selfCheck.a: So you can **invalidate everything at once** by changing the version — old keys become garbage and expire naturally. This is far more reliable than trying to enumerate and delete every affected key during a deploy.

selfCheck.q: **How do you prevent a thundering herd when a hot key expires?**
selfCheck.a: Single-flight / request coalescing (one filler, others wait for its result); refresh-ahead (refresh before expiry); stale-while-revalidate (serve stale, refresh in background); probabilistic early expiration (XFetch); a short TTL with jitter.

selfCheck.q: **Why are `KEYS *` and huge `HGETALL` dangerous in Redis?**
selfCheck.a: Redis executes commands on a single thread. `KEYS *` scans the whole keyspace and blocks every other client for its duration; a huge `HGETALL` blocks during serialization and transfer. Use `SCAN` (incremental) and `HSCAN`/`SSCAN`/`ZSCAN`, `UNLINK` for async deletion, and `lazyfree-lazy-user-del`.

selfCheck.q: **When is a local in-process cache better than Redis?**
selfCheck.a: When the data is read very frequently (hot), the working set fits in local memory, you need the absolute lowest latency (~100 ns vs ~0.5 ms network), and slight per-node staleness is acceptable (with pub/sub invalidation). Not for correctness-critical or large data.

selfCheck.q: **How do you safely deploy a change that alters cached data?**
selfCheck.a: **Version the cache key** (`v2`) so old entries are ignored and expire naturally; use content-hashed asset URLs for the CDN; if you must invalidate, publish invalidation messages over pub/sub and also set a short TTL as a backstop. Verify by checking the new version's hit ratio after deploy.

selfCheck.q: **What is a hot key and how do you mitigate it?**
selfCheck.a: A key receiving a disproportionate share of traffic (a celebrity, a flash-sale item), so one shard/instance becomes a bottleneck. Mitigate with replicas in read mode, sharding the value into sub-keys, moving it to a dedicated instance, or adding a local cache in front of it.
